claims.text: Controlled chemical substitution can enhance electron–phonon coupling in a Nb-based compound.
Sufficiently enhanced electron–phonon coupling can trigger superconductivity below a critical temperature.
The initial Nb-based compound is metallic and non-superconducting at ambient temperature.
Slight chemical doping or substitution, combined with cryogenic cooling, is the proposed intervention.
Doping modifies the crystal lattice of the Nb-based compound.
Doping adjusts bond lengths and angles in the crystal lattice.
Changes in bond lengths and angles tune the phonon spectrum.
Enhanced electron–phonon interactions increase the likelihood of Cooper-pair formation.
Cooper-pair formation occurs below a specific critical temperature.
After chemical tuning and cooling below the critical temperature, the material will exhibit zero electrical resistance.
After chemical tuning and cooling below the critical temperature, the material will exhibit the Meissner effect.
Chemical tuning will improve the superconducting transition temperature relative to the undoped compound.
The undoped Nb-based compound remains metallic and non-superconducting under the same cryogenic conditions.
Superconductivity will appear only below a firm critical temperature.
The appearance of superconductivity is sensitive to the degree of chemical substitution.
The appearance of superconductivity is sensitive to structural integrity.
Excessive doping may disrupt the crystal lattice.
Doping-induced lattice disruption may inhibit superconductivity.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome claims an improved transition temperature relative to the undoped compound, but the baseline is said to remain non-superconducting and therefore has no stated superconducting transition temperature to improve upon.

The predicted outcome calls for an improved transition temperature, which conventionally means a higher Tc, whereas the falsification rule tests for transitions at temperatures lower than the baseline material.
